title: Memory Concepts
content_html:
Memory Concepts

Concept Why it matters Application idea
Working Memory Architecture Clarifies how information is temporarily maintained and manipulated (central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad), shaping UI affordances and task design. Add on‑screen 'scratchpads' tied to audio/visual buffers; throttle parameter sliders to simulate capacity limits.
Episodic vs Semantic Memory Separates event‑based, self‑related remembering from general knowledge; useful for modeling 'scene' presets vs. learned rules. Maintain dual stores: episodic render manifests for specific runs vs. semantic presets distilled from many runs.
Schema‑Accelerated Consolidation Prior knowledge speeds integration of new information; design presets/schemas that make new material 'stick' faster. Allow users to define 'schema profiles' (color/geometry rules). New inputs get tagged as schema‑consistent to fast‑track consolidation to presets.
Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) Explains rapid hippocampal learning vs. slow neocortical integration; guides how to blend fast experiments with slow 'style' learning. Two‑speed learning: a fast 'session memory' and a slow 'style learner' that periodically distills parameters from many sessions.
Temporal Organization (Time Cells) Hippocampal neurons code the flow of time, organizing sequences beyond space. Embed a 'temporal rail' that schedules visual changes independent of spatial layout; export sequence heatmaps.
Cognitive Maps: Place & Grid Cells Spatial coding underpins episodic context and navigation; inspires layout logic for scene exploration. Map parameter 'places' on a 2D grid; let users 'walk' through presets to trigger context‑sensitive transitions.
Pattern Separation & Completion Balances distinguishing similar inputs vs. filling in missing details; crucial for avoiding muddiness in composites. Expose 'separate ↔ complete' slider controlling tolerance for near‑duplicate frames and in‑between inference.
Hippocampal Indexing Theory Hippocampus indexes distributed cortical traces; suggests how to rehydrate complex renders from sparse 'indices'. Store compact 'index' files that can reconstruct full project state via referenced assets and seed hashes.
Reconsolidation (and its Limits) Reactivated memories can become labile and update; informs non‑destructive editing workflows. Open‑on‑recall mode: edits fork a new version while optionally writing deltas back to the 'memory'.
Sleep‑Dependent Consolidation Offline replay stabilizes and reorganizes memories; points to staged processing and 'overnight' jobs. Queue a 'sleep cycle' batch that replays recent runs (TMR‑like cueing via tags) to refine presets.
Emotion & Neuromodulators Arousal and novelty (amygdala, dopamine) gate consolidation; design salience‑aware capture. Weight features by 'novelty' score; add an 'arousal meter' that boosts save priority.
Event Segmentation & Temporal Context We parse continuous experience into events; memory retrieval follows temporal context dynamics. Auto‑detect event boundaries (scene cuts, motion spikes) and index clips by temporal context vectors.
Encoding Specificity & Levels of Processing Recall depends on matched cues and depth/meaning of processing; informs UI for tagging & elaboration. Attach multimodal cues (sound, palette) at import; prompt meaning‑rich annotations to improve later retrieval.
Spacing & Testing Effects (Desirable Difficulties) Spacing and retrieval practice outperform massed study; guides scheduled reviews of assets/settings. Add spaced‑review reminders for presets; include 'self‑test' renders that hide settings until recall.
Metamemory & Control Judgments of learning and feeling‑of‑knowing regulate study and retrieval strategies. Show confidence prompts after renders; adapt spacing/saves based on user‑reported FOK.
Social & Extended Memory Groups distribute memory (transactive memory) and tools can be part of 'mind' (extended mind). Collaborative roles (who remembers what); external notebooks become first‑class 'memory props'.
Engram Cells (Memory Traces) Specific neuron ensembles store and can reinstate memories; illuminates persistence vs. updating. Treat each render as an 'engram ensemble' across modules; allow selective reactivation and rewrite.
Capacity Limits & Chunking System constraints shape interface complexity; chunking increases effective capacity. Group controls into named chunks; limit simultaneous 'active' parameters to a manageable span.

Details & Citations

Working Memory Architecture

Why: Clarifies how information is temporarily maintained and manipulated (central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad), shaping UI affordances and task design.

Application idea: Add on‑screen 'scratchpads' tied to audio/visual buffers; throttle parameter sliders to simulate capacity limits.

Working Memory From the Psychological and Neural Perspective
Baddeley & Hitch (1974)

Episodic vs Semantic Memory

Why: Separates event‑based, self‑related remembering from general knowledge; useful for modeling 'scene' presets vs. learned rules.

Application idea: Maintain dual stores: episodic render manifests for specific runs vs. semantic presets distilled from many runs.

Tulving (2002) Episodic memory: from mind to brain
Renoult et al. (2019) semantic–episodic interface

Schema‑Accelerated Consolidation

Why: Prior knowledge speeds integration of new information; design presets/schemas that make new material 'stick' faster.

Application idea: Allow users to define 'schema profiles' (color/geometry rules). New inputs get tagged as schema‑consistent to fast‑track consolidation to presets.

Tse et al. (2007) Schemata enhance rapid systems consolidation
Ghosh & Gilboa (2014) What is a memory schema?

Complementary Learning Systems (CLS)

Why: Explains rapid hippocampal learning vs. slow neocortical integration; guides how to blend fast experiments with slow 'style' learning.

Application idea: Two‑speed learning: a fast 'session memory' and a slow 'style learner' that periodically distills parameters from many sessions.

McClelland, McNaughton & O’Reilly (1995)
O’Reilly et al. (2014) CLS overview

Temporal Organization (Time Cells)

Why: Hippocampal neurons code the flow of time, organizing sequences beyond space.

Application idea: Embed a 'temporal rail' that schedules visual changes independent of spatial layout; export sequence heatmaps.

Eichenbaum (2014) Time cells review
Eichenbaum (2017) Time & space in hippocampus

Cognitive Maps: Place & Grid Cells

Why: Spatial coding underpins episodic context and navigation; inspires layout logic for scene exploration.

Application idea: Map parameter 'places' on a 2D grid; let users 'walk' through presets to trigger context‑sensitive transitions.

Nobel Prize (2014) — place & grid cells
Burgess (2014) spatial cells in humans

Pattern Separation & Completion

Why: Balances distinguishing similar inputs vs. filling in missing details; crucial for avoiding muddiness in composites.

Application idea: Expose 'separate ↔ complete' slider controlling tolerance for near‑duplicate frames and in‑between inference.

Yassa & Stark (2011) pattern separation review

Hippocampal Indexing Theory

Why: Hippocampus indexes distributed cortical traces; suggests how to rehydrate complex renders from sparse 'indices'.

Application idea: Store compact 'index' files that can reconstruct full project state via referenced assets and seed hashes.

Teyler & DiScenna (1986)
Teyler & Rudy (2007) update

Reconsolidation (and its Limits)

Why: Reactivated memories can become labile and update; informs non‑destructive editing workflows.

Application idea: Open‑on‑recall mode: edits fork a new version while optionally writing deltas back to the 'memory'.

Nader (2015) reconsolidation overview
Kim et al. (2021) scope & controversies

Sleep‑Dependent Consolidation

Why: Offline replay stabilizes and reorganizes memories; points to staged processing and 'overnight' jobs.

Application idea: Queue a 'sleep cycle' batch that replays recent runs (TMR‑like cueing via tags) to refine presets.

Diekelmann & Born (2010) review

Emotion & Neuromodulators

Why: Arousal and novelty (amygdala, dopamine) gate consolidation; design salience‑aware capture.

Application idea: Weight features by 'novelty' score; add an 'arousal meter' that boosts save priority.

McGaugh (2004) amygdala & consolidation
Lisman & Grace (2005) hippocampal‑VTA loop
Duszkiewicz et al. (2019) novelty–dopamine

Event Segmentation & Temporal Context

Why: We parse continuous experience into events; memory retrieval follows temporal context dynamics.

Application idea: Auto‑detect event boundaries (scene cuts, motion spikes) and index clips by temporal context vectors.

Zacks et al. (2007) event segmentation
Howard & Kahana (2002) Temporal Context Model

Encoding Specificity & Levels of Processing

Why: Recall depends on matched cues and depth/meaning of processing; informs UI for tagging & elaboration.

Application idea: Attach multimodal cues (sound, palette) at import; prompt meaning‑rich annotations to improve later retrieval.

Tulving & Thomson (1973) encoding specificity
Craik & Lockhart (1972) levels of processing

Spacing & Testing Effects (Desirable Difficulties)

Why: Spacing and retrieval practice outperform massed study; guides scheduled reviews of assets/settings.

Application idea: Add spaced‑review reminders for presets; include 'self‑test' renders that hide settings until recall.

Cepeda et al. (2006/2008) spacing meta‑analyses
Roediger & Karpicke (2006) testing effect Bjork & Bjork (2011) desirable difficulties

Metamemory & Control

Why: Judgments of learning and feeling‑of‑knowing regulate study and retrieval strategies.

Application idea: Show confidence prompts after renders; adapt spacing/saves based on user‑reported FOK.

Nelson & Narens (1990) metamemory framework

Social & Extended Memory

Why: Groups distribute memory (transactive memory) and tools can be part of 'mind' (extended mind).

Application idea: Collaborative roles (who remembers what); external notebooks become first‑class 'memory props'.

Wegner (1987/1995) transactive memory
Clark & Chalmers (1998) The Extended Mind

Engram Cells (Memory Traces)

Why: Specific neuron ensembles store and can reinstate memories; illuminates persistence vs. updating.

Application idea: Treat each render as an 'engram ensemble' across modules; allow selective reactivation and rewrite.

Tonegawa et al. (2015) engram review
Josselyn & Tonegawa (2020)

Capacity Limits & Chunking

Why: System constraints shape interface complexity; chunking increases effective capacity.

Application idea: Group controls into named chunks; limit simultaneous 'active' parameters to a manageable span.

Miller (1956) Magical Number Seven
Cowan (2015) capacity reappraisal
Gobet (2001) chunking mechanisms
